The company is in the final stage of FAA certification (Stage 5) and is targeting first U.S. eIPP (eVTOL Integration Pilot Program) flights in 2026. It's also flying in Texas as part of a White House-backed pilot program, with a week-long campaign across the Dallas-Fort Worth region, including routes into DFW Airport. Bulls point to the Toyota partnership, manufacturing ramp, and massive liquidity as evidence that Joby is the clear leader in the eVTOL space. Some are calling it a millionaire-maker with a $20 price target, arguing that Joby is launching before full certification by leveraging international regulators and alternate pathways. They also note that cash flow is solid for two years with no dilution needed. On the bearish side, the frustration is palpable. Some posters are furious about the stock's decline, blaming short sellers, BlackRock, and 'illegals algos' in profanity-laced rants. They note that the stock has dropped from $19 to $16 in two days and expect further downside, urging others to buy puts. There's also concern about competition from Archer Aviation (ACHR), which is trading at a slight discount to Joby. One poster bought a starter position at the 52-week low but is hedging by owning both JOBY and ACHR. Overall, the community is deeply divided. The bull case rests on Joby's technological lead, strong balance sheet, and certification progress. The bear case focuses on the long timeline to profitability, regulatory hurdles, and the risk of dilution or failure. For investors, JOBY is a high-risk, high-reward play on the future of urban air mobility. The potential market is enormous, but so are the challenges. The stock is volatile, and sentiment can swing wildly. If you believe in the eVTOL story, Joby is arguably the best-positioned pure-play, but don't bet the farm—this is still a speculative bet on a technology that hasn't yet proven it can scale commercially.

BABA.summary: Alibaba (BABA) is getting almost no attention on Reddit right now, with zero mentions in the last 24 hours and no rank on the retail radar. That silence is itself a signal: the meme-stock crowd that once piled into Chinese tech has largely moved on. On Stocktwits, the mood is overwhelmingly negative, with 24 bearish tags versus just 8 bullish ones. The messages are dominated by frustrated long-term holders and outright mockery. One user says they bought BABA instead of Amazon in 2017 and will never buy China again. Another complains that Chinese stocks don't rise with the US market but fall right along with it, calling it 'pure junk' after holding for six years. Several posts are from a single very vocal bear who repeatedly calls BABA a 'value trap' and mocks retail bulls as 'moronic dumbo bulltards' who don't understand opportunity cost. That user claims to be Chinese and insists the stock will keep sagging. The few positive comments are drowned out: one says all Chinese stocks are buys at 'insane valuations,' but it got only five likes. The bearish posts often get three or more likes, showing agreement. Why is BABA so disliked? It's a mix of China regulatory fears, geopolitical tension, a weak Chinese consumer, and years of disappointing price action. Many investors who bought the 2020 hype at $250+ are still deep underwater and have lost patience. The stock is seen as a value trap: cheap on paper but never recovering. Bulls argue the valuation is too low to ignore, but bears counter that opportunity cost is huge—money tied up in BABA could have been in US tech. For investors, the key takeaway is that sentiment is extremely poor, which can sometimes mark a bottom, but there's no clear catalyst. Watch China's stimulus measures, regulatory changes, and Alibaba's cloud and e-commerce growth. If you're bullish, you need a strong stomach and a long time horizon. If you're bearish, you're in good company on Stocktwits. Either way, do your own research—this is not financial advice.
